intro: Near LaCrosse, about 19 km north-west of Gainesville, Alachua County keeps ten acres of mown lawn for a single live oak. The Cellon Oak is 91 feet tall with a trunk 390 inches round, about 9.9 metres, and a crown spreading 171 feet, by the state champion tree register's 2018 measurement. It is listed as Florida's co-champion live oak and is put at more than 200 years. In 2025 the county closed the park for two days to fit new lightning protection. You need a car to get there.
meta_description: The Cellon Oak near LaCrosse, Florida: a co-champion live oak 91 feet tall in its own county park, about 19 km north-west of Gainesville.
question_meta: Is the Cellon Oak still Florida's champion live oak? What the register says, what changed in 2022, and how to reach it from Gainesville.
question_answer: Not on its own. The Florida Forest Service register lists the Cellon Oak as Florida's co-champion live oak, measured in 2018 at 390 inches round, 91 feet tall and with a crown of 171 feet. In October 2022, WUFT reported, the title passed to a live oak on private land elsewhere in Alachua with a thicker trunk, 36.5 feet round. The Cellon Oak is still about 13 feet the taller of the two.
question_context: The tree that took the title in 2022 is 78 feet tall with a crown of 180 feet and stands on private land. The Cellon Oak stands in a county park, bought by Alachua County in 1989 and free to enter. The park is little more than the tree. A ten-acre mown lawn surrounds it, with two picnic tables and a grill and no restrooms. Its age is an estimate. A 2019 WUFT caption put its planting at about 1832, a local television station says more than 200 years, and nobody has cored it. Lightning is the county's main worry, and in April 2025 it shut the park for two days to install a new protection system. You will see the name spelled Ceylon in some older reports; Cellon is the park's own spelling. The park lies near LaCrosse, about 19 km north-west of central Gainesville. We found no public transport, so plan on a car, and confirm the hours before you go.

faq.q: How far is the Cellon Oak from Gainesville?
faq.a: About 19 km north-west of central Gainesville and the University of Florida, near LaCrosse. No public transport goes there that we could find, so it is a drive.

faq.q: How big is the Cellon Oak?
faq.a: The state champion tree register measured it in 2018 at 390 inches round, about 9.9 metres, 91 feet tall, with a crown spreading 171 feet.

faq.q: Is it Cellon Oak or Ceylon Oak?
faq.a: Both spellings appear. Older press reports and a university fact sheet write Ceylon; the register and the park itself use Cellon.

trees.story:
Alachua County bought ten acres in 1989 for the sake of one tree, and the park is still just that. A mown lawn, two picnic tables, a grill and the Cellon Oak.

The Florida Forest Service's champion tree register measured it in 2018 at 390 inches around, about 9.9 metres, 91 feet tall, with a crown spreading 171 feet. The register lists it as Florida's co-champion live oak. In October 2022, WUFT reported, the title passed to a live oak on private land elsewhere in Alachua with a thicker trunk, 36.5 feet round. The Cellon Oak is still about 13 feet the taller of the two.

Its age is an estimate. A 2019 WUFT caption put its planting at about 1832, a local television station says more than 200 years, and nobody has cored it. A blog's 300 to 500 years has nothing behind it.

Lightning is what worries the county. In April 2025 it closed the park for two days to fit a new lightning protection system, meant to keep a strike from killing the tree.

You will see the name spelled Ceylon in some older reports. Cellon is the park's own spelling. The park lies near LaCrosse, about 19 km north-west of central Gainesville and the University of Florida. We found no public transport, so plan on a car. Entry is free, a third-party listing gives the hours as 8 in the morning to 7 at night, and there are no restrooms.

trees.access: Free. Alachua County park bought by the county in 1989 (WUFT 2019); a mown 10-acre lawn around a single tree, two picnic tables and a grill, no restrooms. Third-party app lists 8 AM to 7 PM daily (not the county's own page; confirm). Closed 10 to 11 April 2025 for a lightning-protection installation, reopened after (WCJB).
trees.transport: About 19 km north-west of central Gainesville and the University of Florida; no public transport verified. By car only as far as this pass found.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the single tree the park's mown ten-acre lawn is kept around, 91 feet tall with a crown spreading 171 feet. It stands in Cellon Oak Park, near LaCrosse north-west of Gainesville.
trees.verify_notes: FLAGGED: a county park and register plus press, but no photo with a geotag and no public transport. LONG-DAY-TRIP: roughly 19 km (straight line) from UF; rule says within about 30 minutes by public transport; none found, so the writer or queue may prefer to keep it as a lone tree page. ALIVE: lifecheck RECENT 2026-10-31 (iNaturalist, https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/412314976, within about 150 m of the register point); WCJB 2025-04-10: Alachua County Parks and Open Space installed a new lightning protection system to keep lightning from killing the tree. SIZE: register 2018 measurement as seen on the register's public ArcGIS layer: circumference 390 inches (991 cm), height 91 ft (27.7 m), crown spread 171 ft; WCJB 2025: measures more than 32 feet around and about 91 feet high; WUFT 2019: 91 ft tall, circumference more than 30 ft. A 2019/2023 WUFT piece says it is the Florida co-champion; WUFT 2023: the title passed in October 2022 to a bigger-trunked live oak on private land in Alachua (36.5 ft around, 78 ft tall, crown 180 ft); Cellon Oak is about 13 ft taller. Species size check: 991 cm is 118% of the species reference of 843 cm (n=11, species_size.py). AGE: WCJB: more than 200 years old (no source named); WUFT 2019 caption: estimated planted in 1832 and calls it a 187-year-old tree; an unattributed blog says 300 to 500 years, rejected as unsupported (same blog says no way to age it without killing it). Nobody cored it. Held broad. CONDITION per blog (not a source for facts): lightning rods, cable support for a large limb. NOTE: the register spells the place Cellon, WUFT 2015 and a UF fact sheet spell it Ceylon; Cellon is the park's name. PIN: register coordinate in a single-tree park; no aerial check or geotagged photo this pass, so approximate. No Commons photo exists (searched Cellon Oak and geosearch within 400 m, none).
